notable_qa.question: Inquired about the timeline for the normalization of the 5 million barrels of refinery capacity impacted in Russia and the Middle East, estimating 6 to 9 months in a best-case scenario or longer.
notable_qa.answer: Management stated that uncertainty is very high due to continuing attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and low inventories, and they do not see an immediate change in the situation.
supporting_quotes: So is it fair to assume this 5 million barrels is probably six to nine months away from normalization in a best case scenario, and worst case it could be it could stretch for even longer?

notable_qa.question: Inquired whether structural demand destruction in China due to rapid adoption of EVs and LNG as fuel would lead to permanently lower refining margins.
notable_qa.answer: Management acknowledged China's structural shift to EVs and LNG trucks, but noted that demand growth in the rest of the world will offset it, and historical market memories of supply shocks will prevent normalisation of margins and freight.
supporting_quotes: I am just wondering is there a structural destruction of demand and if we go back to a normalized level will we actually see refining margins lower than the previous normalized levels

notable_qa.question: Asked whether online grocery growth is underwhelming compared to quick commerce players and if the target of doubling EBITDA in two years remains confident, as well as inquiring about O2C spread capture improvements.
notable_qa.answer: Management reaffirmed the target to double EBITDA over two years, noting that growth is pursued in a measured, sustainable way leveraging existing infrastructure and a 400-million customer base rather than pure cash burn. For petrochemicals, ethane benefits will increase with incremental vessels, and relaxed LPG control orders helped improve volumes compared to the previous quarter.
supporting_quotes: So, on retail, the revenue growth number for online grocery that has been given about 46% or something this if we compare it to the biggest quick commerce players also, it is still underwhelming, to say the least.
We are not changing ours that is the target that we are going for. There is no reason, at least as of now, for us to change that target.

risks.risk: Inflation is at a two-year high, impacting consumer purchasing power.

risks.quote: Inflation is on a two year high, which is impacting the purchasing power for people.

risks.risk: Significant currency depreciation is impacting the cost of imported products and landed product prices.
risks.speaker: Sh Dinesh Taluja
risks.quote: Currency has depreciated significantly. That is impacting, especially, some of the imported products. The landed products have gone up.

risks.risk: Monsoon deficit has caused demand pressure across key agrarian-dependent states and rising food prices are eating into discretionary demand.
risks.speaker: Sh Dinesh Taluja
risks.quote: Monsoon deficit. So that has caused some demand pressure across some of the key agri dependent states, as well as the food prices are moving up. So that is also eating into the discretionary demand.

risks.risk: Intense competition and discounting from quick commerce in the grocery segment leading to margin pressures.
risks.speaker: Not identified
risks.quote: Now, this is a segment where the competition is the most intense from quick commerce. There is a lot of discounting which is happening. So, we are choosing. There are some margin pressures here because, especially in the metros and bigger cities where quick commerce competition is high, we are going for price parity.
